title: US Consumer Sentiment Plunges in September as Inflation Fears Mount
excerpt: The University of Michigan's sentiment index fell to 47.8 in early September while year-ahead inflation expectations jumped to 4.6%, the highest since June.
body:
• The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index fell to 47.8 in early September from 51.7 in August, missing economists' expectations of about 51.
  • Year-ahead inflation expectations jumped to 4.6% from 4.0%, the highest reading since June, as resurging fuel prices and trade tensions squeezed household outlooks.
  • Expectations for personal finances and business conditions plunged, with sentiment declining among both Democrats and Republicans while independents held steady.
  • Sentiment now sits 16% below February levels and 13% below a year ago, approaching the lowest readings in the survey's history.

Sentiment sinks toward historic lows as inflation fears return

U.S. consumer sentiment deteriorated sharply in early September as rising gasoline prices and trade tensions revived fears of higher inflation, according to a preliminary University of Michigan survey released Friday. The Consumer Sentiment Index dropped to 47.8 from a final reading of 51.7 in August, well below the 51 economists polled by Reuters had expected, and marked the second straight monthly decline.

The pullback was broad. The survey's Current Economic Conditions Index slipped to 50.9 from 51.9, while the Index of Consumer Expectations plunged to 45.8 from 51.5. Sentiment fell among consumers identifying as Democrats and Republicans alike, and was little changed among independents, the survey found.

If the preliminary reading holds in the final September tally due later this month, it would be the second-lowest reading in the survey's history, according to The Wall Street Journal. CNN reported the early-September drop of 7.5% marks the second-lowest reading since the gauge's inception more than 70 years ago, with sentiment this year running below levels seen during the Great Recession and the aftermath of 9/11.

Context & Background

The September slide extends a downward trend that began in August, when the index fell to 51.7 from 55.2 in July. Consumers have been rattled by a resurgence in fuel prices tied to the U.S.-led war with Iran, which has kept energy costs elevated and bled into expectations for the broader economy.

Year-ahead inflation expectations were 3.4% in February, before the Iran conflict began. They have since climbed steadily, reaching 4.6% this month — the highest since June and well above every 2024 reading. Longer-run expectations, measured over five years, edged up to 3.4% from 3.3% in August, ending three consecutive months at 3.3% and remaining above their 2024 range of 2.8% to 3.2%.

"With a resurgence in fuel prices and trade tensions, consumers anticipate greater pressures on their pocketbooks to come."

— Joanne Hsu, director, University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers

The survey's authors note that five-year expectations for business conditions held stable but remain well below historical averages, suggesting consumers believe the emerging risks this month have not yet damaged the long-run outlook.

Impact & Analysis

Rising inflation expectations are more than a mood indicator — economists warn they can become self-fulfilling. When consumers expect prices to keep climbing, they comparison-shop less and demand bigger wage increases, which feeds back into prices. Marketplace noted that the gas pump and the grocery store are the two places where expectations are formed, and both have been flashing warning signs.

The gloom is measurable in household budgets. Consumers' expectations for their own inflation-adjusted incomes have weakened steadily over the past year and a half, and only about 10% of consumers expect their purchasing power to increase in the year ahead. A growing share of Americans now sees inflation as a greater risk to the economy than unemployment: this month, 36% named inflation as the more serious hardship, versus 6% for unemployment. At the start of the year, the split was 23% to 14%.

Overall, sentiment is now 16% below February — before the Iran conflict started — and 13% lower than a year ago. Hsu said year-ahead expectations for both personal finances and business conditions "plunged," a sign that consumers see the squeeze persisting.

Diaspora Angle

Consumer spending drives roughly two-thirds of the U.S. economy, so a sustained sentiment slump matters for hiring and business revenues across sectors where many Indian Americans work, from technology to retail. For households, the practical read-through is caution: rising inflation expectations tend to show up in grocery bills and gas receipts before anywhere else, and weaker expectations often precede slower hiring — worth factoring into big-ticket decisions this fall.

What's Next

The final September reading lands later this month and will confirm whether the early-month plunge sticks. More immediately, Federal Reserve officials meet September 15-16 with inflation expectations running hot, and the August PCE inflation report — the Fed's preferred gauge — arrives September 30. Any sign that consumer expectations are stabilizing would give policymakers breathing room; another leg up would not.
